title: Message Tuning Outshines Graph Prompt Tuning
one_liner: Instead of tuning prompts on frozen graph models, inject small learnable message prototypes into each layer to outperform prompt tuning in theory and in practice.
lead: Graph models trained on huge unlabeled networks are now being adapted to solve new graph tasks. The standard method is graph prompt tuning: you craft a prompt (a special input prefix) and tune it while keeping the model weights frozen. This paper proves that approach has a hard upper limit on how much it can adapt. The paper then proposes Message Tuning, which instead injects small learnable message prototypes at each layer, and proves this can exceed prompt tuning's theoretical ceiling.

problem.h2: Graph models are frozen but tasks keep changing
paras: Graph Foundation Models (large models trained on huge networks) are now common. When you need to solve a new graph task, you cannot retrain the whole model—it is too expensive and might forget what it already learned. So you freeze the model and only tune something small.

The standard approach is graph prompt tuning: you add a short special input prefix (the prompt) and tune only that prefix while keeping all model weights frozen. It works because the prompt, placed at the start, shapes all downstream computations—but people did not know whether there was a better way, or how much room to improve remained.

A beginner might just try: add a tunable prompt and let training find the best one. This works for some tasks, but the paper proves that no matter how clever you make the prompt, there is an iron ceiling—a mathematical hard limit—on how much a frozen model can adapt using only input prompts.

callout.b: The paper's move in one sentence.
callout.html: Instead of tuning an input prompt, inject small learnable message prototypes into each layer of the graph model so the model has adjustment points throughout the network, and prove this can adapt beyond what prompt tuning allows because it has more places to steer.

steps.text: Develop Prismatic Space Theory: a math framework that assigns a score to how much any adaptation method can change the model's behavior.
Show mathematically that graph prompt tuning cannot adapt beyond a specific upper bound, even with unlimited computing.
Add learnable message prototypes to each layer to steer the signal fusion at every depth; with adjustment points throughout the network, the model can produce more different outputs on the new task.
Using Prismatic Space Theory, prove that injecting prototypes at every layer can adapt beyond the prompt-tuning bound.
Test on diverse graph datasets and show message tuning consistently beats graph prompt tuning in practice.

object.h2: What changes: the message fusion rule
paras: In a graph neural network, at each layer a node reads messages from its neighbors and fuses them into a new signal. Normally, the way you fuse (the function that combines the neighbor messages) is fixed—it came from pretraining.

Message Tuning inserts a small learnable prototype into this fusion step at every layer. Instead of always fusing the same way, the prototypes act as tunable guides: the network learns to blend the neighbor signals using these prototypes, without changing any of the original frozen weights.

hidden.h2: Adaptation capacity: how much can the model really change?
hidden.name: adaptation capacity
paras: Adaptation capacity is a number that measures how much an adaptation method can alter a frozen model's behavior on a new task. If the capacity is low, the method is weak; if high, it has room to solve very different tasks.

Prismatic Space Theory defines and measures capacity mathematically. The theory shows that prompt tuning has a hard ceiling (a specific capacity value), and that ceiling depends only on the prompt size and the model architecture. Message Tuning's capacity is computed the same way, but the paper proves it can be higher because prototypes at every layer give more 'knobs' to turn.
The paper estimates capacity by analyzing what different outputs the adaptation method can produce when applied to the frozen model—the wider the range of possible outputs, the higher the capacity.

heat.caption: Darker means more adaptation capacity available. Injecting at every layer builds up capacity; prompt only stays narrow.

reads.html: Adaptation capacity is how much freedom the adaptation method gives the model to behave differently on the new task, measured as a mathematical upper bound on the variety of outputs it can produce.

Capacity is formalized in Prismatic Space Theory as the dimensionality of the subspace of model behaviors accessible via the adaptation method, with an explicit upper bound derived from the number of tunable values and how they interact.

mechanism.h2: Why injecting prototypes at every layer beats prompt tuning
paras: Graph prompt tuning adds one adjustable piece (the prompt) at the very front of the network. No matter how well you tune that prompt, it has to work for all layers downstream—all the frozen layers get the same initial nudge, and nothing changes after that first step. Mathematically, this limits the variety of outputs the model can produce on the new task. The adjustment can only happen once, at the beginning.

Message Tuning adds small learnable prototypes inside each layer's message fusion. Now, at layer 1, the model fuses neighbor signals using prototype 1; at layer 2, it uses prototype 2; and so on. Each prototype can be tuned independently. This means the model has many more adjustment points—one per layer. With more adjustment points, the network can adapt to solve more different kinds of new tasks. Mathematically, the space of behaviors the model can reach becomes larger.

The reason this works: in a graph network, the key operation at each layer is message passing (collecting signals from neighbors and blending them). By controlling how the blending happens at every layer, the model gets multiple opportunities to steer its computation toward the new task. Prompt tuning only steers at the start.

stages.s: Task prediction (node labels / link predictions / graph classification)

math.words: The upper bound on adaptation capacity grows with the number of prototypes and the feature dimension they operate on, and is higher for message tuning than for prompt tuning because prototypes are injected at every layer.
math.equation: C_MTG = sum_{l=1}^{L} K_l * D  vs  C_prompt = K * D
symbols: size of learnable prototype at layer l
feature dimension of the graph model

worked.title: A tiny worked example with numbers
lines: Suppose the model has 3 layers, feature dimension D=64, and prompt size K=8.
Message tuning with prototypes of size 8 at each layer: C_MTG = (8*64) + (8*64) + (8*64) = 512 + 512 + 512 = 1536.
Message tuning provides 3x the adaptation capacity because you get knobs at all 3 layers instead of just the input.

math.note: The formula shows why injecting prototypes at multiple layers beats a single prompt: capacity scales linearly with the number of layers in message tuning, but is fixed in prompt tuning.

bars.h2: Adaptation capacity in action: two tasks

charts.title: Prompt tuning
charts.note: Prompt tuning hits its ceiling early; the adaptation method is already at maximum capacity, so performance plateaus.

charts.title: Message tuning
charts.note: Message tuning has higher capacity, so it can adapt more aggressively to the new task while staying within bounds.

items.html: If the prototypes are too small, you do not get enough extra capacity; if too large, tuning becomes unstable or overfits to the new task, erasing what the model learned before.
Injecting prototypes at every layer adds cost. If you skip some layers (to save compute), you lose capacity gains in those layers. Choosing which layers to inject into is a trade-off.

Even with higher capacity, if the new task is radically different from the pretraining task (e.g., predicting chemical properties on a knowledge graph after pretraining on social networks), the gain is smaller.

Message Tuning is designed for moderate adaptation: the new task is related to pretraining but not identical. In this regime, the extra adjustment points per layer give the network more ways to steer behavior toward the new task, so it consistently outperforms prompt tuning.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Take a pretrained graph model and a new downstream task (e.g., node classification on a different network than pretraining saw). Split the task data into train and test.
Train prompt tuning on the training set, recording the best validation accuracy reached. This is the 'ceiling' for prompt tuning.
Now train message tuning with the same budget (same total number of tunable values), injecting prototypes at each layer. Run it on the same training/test split.

Plot the two learning curves side by side: as you train, does message tuning exceed prompt tuning's best validation accuracy? Can it fit the training set more thoroughly because it has more steering points, and does it generalize to the test set better because those extra adjustments guide the frozen layers toward the new task? That is the demo's burden of proof.
demo.closing: The demo must show that message tuning, starting from the same frozen model, reaches higher accuracy on the new task than prompt tuning can, because it has more adaptation knobs per layer.
